SOC action: confirm with the app owner whether they added the secret; if not, remove it immediately, audit every mailbox the app can reach for what was actually accessed and review the app's permission grant. Mail.ReadWrite on an app most owners added for a narrower purpose is itself worth tightening. Known false positives: legitimate CI/CD or integration pipelines that rotate app secrets on a schedule and immediately resume normal mailbox automation. Exclude those app IDs once confirmed.
kql:
let lookback = 30d;
let secret_additions =
    AuditLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where OperationName has_any ("Add service principal credentials", "Update application", "Certificates and secrets management")
    | where Result == "success"
    | mv-expand TargetResources
    | extend AppId   = tolower(tostring(TargetResources.id)),
             AppName = tostring(TargetResources.displayName),
             Actor   = tolower(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)),
             ActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
    | where isnotempty(AppId)
    | project AppId, AppName, Actor, ActorIp, SecretAddedAt = TimeGenerated;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType has_any ("MailItemsAccessed", "Send", "MessageBind")
| extend AppId = tolower(OAuthAppId)
| where isnotempty(AppId)
| join kind=inner secret_additions on AppId
| where Timestamp > SecretAddedAt
| summarize
    MailboxActions = count(),
    Mailboxes      = dcount(AccountObjectId),
    Addresses      = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
    Actions        = make_set(ActionType, 5),
    FirstUse       = min(Timestamp),
    LastUse        = max(Timestamp)
    by AppId, AppName, Actor, ActorIp, SecretAddedAt
| where FirstUse between (SecretAddedAt .. SecretAddedAt + 7d)
| sort by SecretAddedAt desc

name: Device Code Authentication Rarity Hunt
desc: Baseline hunting query, not an alert: lists every account that successfully completed a device code sign-in in the last 30 days. Device code grant is a flow for devices with limited input, so in most tenants it is unused or limited to a small known set of clients and people, which is what makes any new appearance worth reading. Part of the device code phishing-as-a-service surge reported mid-2026. Complements the GoXDR query that ties device code to a subsequent device registration. This one has no correlation gate and is a rarity census. MITRE ATT&CK: T1528 (Steal Application Access Token). SOC action: for each hit, confirm the user and app against your known legitimate device code use cases (CLI tools, IoT, conference room devices). Anything outside that list warrants a direct check with the user. Known limitation: the sign-in record itself shows nothing deceptive because the victim genuinely authenticated, so this only narrows where to look. It does not confirm compromise.
kql:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProtocol =~ "deviceCode"
    or ResultType == "70016"
| extend Country = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| extend City    = tostring(LocationDetails.city)
| summarize
    Attempts    = count(),
    Successes   = countif(ResultType == "0"),
    Apps        = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10),
    Resources   = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10),
    Addresses   = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
    Countries   = make_set(Country, 5),
    UserAgents  = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
    FirstSeen   = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen    = max(TimeGenerated)
    by UserPrincipalName
| where Successes > 0
| sort by FirstSeen desc

name: Token Use From a Different Country After Interactive Sign-In
desc: Joins an interactive sign-in to a non-interactive token use event for the same account within 24 hours, then flags pairs where the countries differ. When a token is stolen rather than a password, the original authentication event stays clean. The compromise only shows up in the gap between where the user signed in and where the token later gets used, which is exactly the pattern device code phishing produces. MITRE ATT&CK: T1528 (Steal Application Access Token). SOC action: check UseApps and Resources for anything the user would not normally run, then revoke refresh tokens for the account and force reauthentication. Known limitation: country comparison is coarse. An operator in the same country as the victim produces nothing. VPN or corporate proxy egress in a different country from the user's real location is a realistic false positive, so check UseIPs against known corporate egress ranges before escalating.
kql:
let huntWindow = 7d;
let interactive =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(huntWindow)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | project UserPrincipalName, AuthTime = TimeGenerated,
              AuthIP      = IPAddress,
              AuthCountry = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion),
              AuthApp     = AppDisplayName;
let tokenUse =
    AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(huntWindow)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | project UserPrincipalName, UseTime = TimeGenerated,
              UseIP      = IPAddress,
              UseCountry = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion),
              UseApp     = AppDisplayName,
              UseResource = ResourceDisplayName;
interactive
| join kind=inner tokenUse on UserPrincipalName
| where UseTime between (AuthTime .. AuthTime + 24h)
| where UseCountry != AuthCountry and isnotempty(UseCountry) and isnotempty(AuthCountry)
| summarize    Uses       = count(),
    UseApps    = make_set(UseApp, 10),
    Resources  = make_set(UseResource, 10),
    UseIPs     = make_set(UseIP, 10),
    FirstUse   = min(UseTime)
    by UserPrincipalName, AuthTime, AuthIP, AuthCountry, UseCountry
| sort by FirstUse desc

name: Device Login Page Link Clicked From Email or Teams
desc: Flags a click on a genuine Microsoft device login URL that arrived through email or Teams. A device login page is something a user reaches because a device in front of them displayed a code, not something that should arrive as a link in a message, so the combination of that exact destination with a mail/chat origin is the anomaly. The domain itself is legitimate Microsoft infrastructure and will not trip a malicious URL detector. SOC action: pull the sender and subject for context, treat as an active device code phishing attempt and pair this with the sign-in rarity hunt for the same user around the same timestamp, then warn the user before they enter any code. MITRE ATT&CK: T1566 (Phishing), T1204.001 (User Execution: Malicious Link). Known limitation: this depends on Safe Links rewriting and click telemetry. A device code link delivered through a channel outside that protection (an unmonitored chat app, a QR code, a phone call) will not appear here at all.
kql:
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any (
      "microsoft.com/devicelogin",
      "login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/deviceauth",
      "aka.ms/devicelogin")
| where Workload in ("Email", "Teams")
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, UrlDomain, Url) on $left.NetworkMessageId == $right.NetworkMessageId
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, Subject, EmailDirection) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, Workload,
          SenderFromAddress, Subject, EmailDirection, IPAddress
| sort by Timestamp desc

name: AI Coding Assistant CLI Launched With Permission-Bypass Flags
desc: Hunting query, not an alert. Detects AI coding assistant CLIs (Claude Code, Amazon Q CLI, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI) launched with flags that skip permission prompts, bypass approvals or disable the sandbox. Runs with a scripted parent or non-interactive mode are sorted first, since nobody is watching the agent in those cases. MITRE ATT&CK: no precise technique exists for this class. T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter) is the closest mapping. MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0103 (Deploy AI Agent), closest mapping. SOC action: read the command line and parent chain, then check what the agent was pointed at and whether the device holds production credentials or source. Known false positives: developers and CI jobs using these flags in disposable containers or VMs. Limitation: matching is on literal command-line text, so modes set through a config file or an environment variable are not caught, and neither is the permission mode bypassPermissions form of Claude Code.
kql:
// AI coding assistant CLIs launched with permission-bypass flags. Hunting query, not an alert.
// Developers use these flags legitimately. Review the parent chain and command line.
let Lookback = 14d;
let Runtimes = dynamic(["node", "node.exe", "npm", "npm.exe", "npx", "npx.exe", "python", "python3", "python.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "--dangerously-skip-permissions"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--trust-all-tools"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--yolo"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"--approval-mode[ =]yolo"
| extend Tool = case(
    ProcessCommandLine contains "--dangerously-skip-permissions", "Claude Code",
    ProcessCommandLine contains "--trust-all-tools", "Amazon Q CLI",
    ProcessCommandLine contains "--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox", "Codex CLI",
    ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"--approval-mode[ =]yolo", "Gemini CLI",
    "Codex CLI or Gemini CLI (--yolo)")
| extend NonInteractive = ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(^|\s)(-p|--print|--prompt|--no-interactive)(\s|=|$)"
| extend ScriptedParent = InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (Runtimes) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (Runtimes)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Tool, ScriptedParent, NonInteractive, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| sort by ScriptedParent desc, NonInteractive desc, Timestamp desc

name: Accounts Still Signing In With Authenticated SMTP
desc: Inventory query, not an alert. Lists accounts that still sign in successfully with Authenticated SMTP over the last 30 days. Microsoft plans to disable Basic auth for SMTP AUTH by default for existing tenants at the end of December 2026. Admins will still be able to turn it back on. Rows come from SigninLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, grouped per account with successful sign-in count, source IP count, apps and first and last seen. MITRE ATT&CK: T1078.004 (Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts) is the related risk, since SMTP AUTH cannot prompt for MFA. SOC action: find the owner of each account, then move the sender to OAuth or a mail relay before the change. Limitations: covers only sign-ins that reach the logs. The Protocols column shows the Entra grant type, not the Basic or Modern Auth split of the Exchange report. Cross check with the Exchange admin center SMTP AUTH Clients report, which supports a date range up to 90 days.
kql:
// Accounts still signing in with Authenticated SMTP. Inventory query, not an alert.
// Run before SMTP AUTH is disabled. Find the owner, then move the sender to OAuth or a relay.
let Lookback = 30d;
union isfuzzy=true SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ClientAppUsed =~ "Authenticated SMTP"
| where ResultType == "0"
| summarize Successes = count(), SourceIps = dcount(IPAddress), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5),
    Protocols = make_set(tostring(column_ifexists("AuthenticationProtocol", "")), 5),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by UserPrincipalName
| sort by Successes desc

name: Guests Holding a Directory Role or Sensitive Group
desc: Hunting query, not an alert. Lists guest accounts that hold an Entra directory role or sit in a group whose name looks sensitive, using the latest IdentityInfo row per account from the last 14 days. A guest with a directory role is the finding that matters most. Group matching is a name keyword heuristic (admin, finance, payroll, legal, exec, board, confiden, security, privileg), so expect some noise and tune the list to your naming. The query handles both IdentityInfo schemas (AccountUPN or AccountUpn, UserType or TenantMembershipType). GroupMembership needs Sentinel UEBA. MITRE ATT&CK: T1078.004 (Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts) is the related risk. SOC action: confirm the business owner of each guest and the reason for the role, then remove the role or group membership if there is none. Prefer time bound access through PIM over a standing assignment. Known false positives: partner or MSP admins with a documented standing role. Groups that match a keyword without being sensitive are another source.
kql:
// Guests holding a directory role or sitting in a sensitive group. Hunting query, not an alert.
let IdentityLookback = 14d;
IdentityInfo
| where TimeGenerated > ago(IdentityLookback)
| extend Upn = tolower(coalesce(column_ifexists("AccountUPN", ""), column_ifexists("AccountUpn", "")))
| extend MemberType = coalesce(column_ifexists("UserType", ""), column_ifexists("TenantMembershipType", ""))
| where MemberType =~ "Guest" and isnotempty(Upn)
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, Upn, IsAccountEnabled, AccountDisplayName, AssignedRoles, GroupMembership) by AccountObjectId
| extend Roles = tostring(AssignedRoles), Groups = tostring(GroupMembership)
| extend HasDirectoryRole = isnotempty(Roles) and Roles !in ("[]", "null", "")
| extend SensitiveGroups = extract_all(@"(?i)([^""\[\],]*(?:admin|finance|payroll|legal|exec|board|confiden|security|privileg)[^""\[\],]*)", Groups)
| where HasDirectoryRole or array_length(SensitiveGroups) > 0
| extend HomeDomain = coalesce(extract(@"(?i)_([^_]+)#ext#", 1, Upn), tostring(split(Upn, "@")[1]))
| project Upn, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, HomeDomain, IsAccountEnabled, HasDirectoryRole, AssignedRoles, SensitiveGroups
| sort by HasDirectoryRole desc, array_length(SensitiveGroups) desc

name: Dormant Guest Accounts With No Recent Sign-In
desc: Hunting query, not an alert. Lists guest accounts with no successful sign-in in the last 90 days or whose last one is at least 30 days old, privileged guests first. Sign-ins come from SigninLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs and are matched to IdentityInfo on the object ID, because the UPN of a guest can differ between sign-in logs and the user object. DaysSilent of 9999 means no successful sign-in at all in the window. Silent is not proof of abandonment. Guests who use resources a few times a year (auditors, partners, quarterly processes) will appear. A guest whose sign-ins keep failing is also listed as silent. MITRE ATT&CK: T1078.004 (Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts) is the related risk, since an unused guest with access is an unmonitored entry point. SOC action: contact the sponsor or inviter of each guest, then block sign-in first and delete only after a waiting period. Deleted users can be restored for 30 days. Treat that as a safety net and not as a plan. Limitations: Lookback must not exceed the retention of both sign-in tables. The query fails if either table is missing, which is intended so that a data gap cannot pass as dormancy. GroupMembership needs Sentinel UEBA.

name: Entra Agent User PIM Role Activation or Assignment
desc: Flags Privileged Identity Management (PIM) role activations and assignments (eligible or active) where the actor or the target is an Entra Agent ID identity. An agent is matched by the agentType field, by a blueprintId value or by a UPN you add to the AgentUpns list. Agent users look like normal Member accounts. A PIM role on one is easy to miss in a standard PIM review. MITRE ATT&CK: T1098.003 (Additional Cloud Roles), T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts). SOC action: confirm with the agent owner whether the role is intended, check who made the assignment (SelfInitiated shows an agent activating its own role) and review what the role can reach. If it is not intended, remove the assignment and review the agent's recent sign-ins. Known limitations: agentType in TargetResources is the documented field used by the Agent User Added to Group query, but agentType in InitiatedBy and blueprintId are not confirmed in Microsoft documentation and population is inconsistent while Entra Agent ID is in preview. The UPN list is the reliable signal, so an empty result is not proof that no agent holds a role. Validate the PIM OperationName strings in your tenant before relying on this. Hunting query, not an alert. Use a 1d lookback to run it as a scheduled rule.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert. Use 1d for a scheduled rule
// NOTE: Replace domain.com with your agent user UPNs
let AgentUpns = dynamic(["agent-user@domain.com"]);
let Lookback = 90d;
let PimOps = dynamic([
    "Add member to role completed (PIM activation)",
    "Add eligible member to role in PIM completed (permanent)",
    "Add eligible member to role in PIM completed (timebound)",
    "Add member to role in PIM completed (permanent)",
    "Add member to role in PIM completed (timebound)"
]);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where OperationName in (PimOps)
| extend Init = tostring(InitiatedBy), Tgt = tostring(TargetResources)
| extend AgentTypes = array_concat(
    coalesce(extract_all(@'"agentType":\s*"([^"]+)"', Init), dynamic([])),
    coalesce(extract_all(@'"agentType":\s*"([^"]+)"', Tgt), dynamic([])))
| extend AgentTypesFound = set_difference(AgentTypes, dynamic(["notAgentic"]))
| extend ByType = array_length(AgentTypesFound) > 0
| extend ByBlueprint = Init matches regex @'"blueprintId":\s*"[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}"'
    or Tgt matches regex @'"blueprintId":\s*"[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}"'
| extend ByList = Init has_any (AgentUpns) or Tgt has_any (AgentUpns)
| where ByType or ByBlueprint or ByList
| mv-apply t = parse_json(Tgt) on (
    summarize
        TargetUser = take_anyif(tostring(t.userPrincipalName), tostring(t.type) == "User"),
        RoleName = take_anyif(tostring(t.displayName), tostring(t.type) == "Role"))
| extend ActorUpn = tostring(parse_json(Init).user.userPrincipalName)
| extend Actor = coalesce(ActorUpn, tostring(parse_json(Init).app.displayName))
| extend Activity = iff(OperationName has "PIM activation", "Role activation", iff(OperationName has "eligible", "Eligible assignment", "Active assignment"))
| extend SelfInitiated = isnotempty(Actor) and tolower(Actor) == tolower(TargetUser)
| project TimeGenerated, Activity, RoleName, Actor, ActorUpn, TargetUser, SelfInitiated, AgentTypesFound, ByType, ByBlueprint, ByList, Result, CorrelationId
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

name: Entra Service Principal Sign-Ins From Stolen App Credentials Hunt
desc: Hunts for service principals signing in with valid but stolen application credentials, based on the November 2026 campaign where an actor used harvested client secrets to sign in as workload identities. Three signals come back in one result set. The first matches the reported operator IP and two client strings. The second finds an invalid or expired client secret error (7000215 or 7000222) followed by a successful sign-in for the same app from the same IP within 15 minutes, which fits an actor working through harvested secrets. The third lists apps whose first successful sign-in falls inside the lookback with none earlier in the 30 day window. MITRE ATT&CK: T1078.004 (Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts). SOC action: for any hit, rotate the app's secrets and federated credentials, review its role assignments and Graph application permissions and check what the app accessed after the sign-in. Known false positives: a new or dormant app signing in for the first time and a developer retrying from one IP after fixing an expired secret. Known limitation: the IP and client strings are a snapshot that the actor can change, so the failure then success pattern is the durable signal. Requires the EntraIdSpnSignInEvents table in Defender advanced hunting, which needs a Microsoft Entra ID P2 license. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: Telegram Bot API Connections Outside the Telegram Client Hunt
desc: Hunts for processes that connect to the Telegram Bot API (api.telegram.org) other than the Telegram desktop client. Malware and scripts use the Bot API as a command and control or data exfiltration channel because the traffic is HTTPS to a widely allowed host. Results are grouped by device, process and account with the URLs, remote IPs and command lines seen. MITRE ATT&CK: T1102 (Web Service), T1567 (Exfiltration Over Web Service). SOC action: review the initiating process path, signer and command line, look for a bot token in the command line or script and check which files the process touched before the connections. Known false positives: IT automation, alerting scripts, monitoring tools and developer tooling that post to Telegram bots. Known limitation: the client exclusion relies on the file name and the version info company name, which an attacker can copy, so also review telegram.exe running outside its expected install path. Hunting query, not an alert.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert
let Lookback = 7d;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org"
// Regex confirms the host boundary after the has prefilter
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)(^|//|\.)api\.telegram\.org(:\d+)?(/|$)"
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "telegram.exe" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Telegram")
| summarize Events = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Urls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 5), RemoteIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 5), CommandLines = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 3), arg_max(Timestamp, ReportId, DeviceId) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| project Timestamp, ReportId, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Events, FirstSeen, Urls, RemoteIPs, CommandLines
| order by Timestamp desc

name: Trojanized Claude Code Extension SSH Backdoor Hunt
desc: Hunts for indicators of the trojanized Claude Code extension that was served through the Cursor Marketplace and disclosed on 30 October 2026 (reported versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313). The malicious build planted an SSH backdoor with a reverse tunnel to a fixed host, an added authorized key and persistence files on macOS, Linux and Windows. Three checks run over 30 days. The first looks for connections to the tunnel host. The second looks for ssh or autossh with a reverse forward to local port 22 or the tunnel user and host. The third looks for the hash of the injected extension.js and the dropped persistence files. Results are grouped per device and signal. MITRE ATT&CK: T1195.002 (Compromise Software Supply Chain), T1572 (Protocol Tunneling), T1098.004 (SSH Authorized Keys). SOC action: isolate the device, remove the extension and the persistence files, delete the injected key from authorized_keys, rotate credentials and keys reachable from the host and review inbound SSH logs for sessions from the tunnel host. Known false positives: administrators using a reverse SSH forward to port 22 for legitimate remote support. Known limitation: the hunt covers published indicators only and file events depend on Defender sensor coverage. Other distribution channels of the extension were reported unaffected. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: Teams External Chat Hunt: Fake IT Support Senders and Known Campaign Tenants
desc: Hunts for external Teams chats where the sender looks like IT support or comes from a throwaway tenant used in the fake help desk campaigns. The pattern is a mailbox flood, then a chat from an attacker tenant posing as IT support and a follow up call that gets the user to start Quick Assist or another remote tool. The query flags external threads where the sender display name matches help desk lure wording or the sender domain is on the reported tenant list, then groups per sender with recipient count, thread count, threat verdicts and a KnownIndicatorTenant flag. MITRE ATT&CK: T1566.003 (Phishing: Spearphishing via Service), T1656 (Impersonation). SOC action: contact the targeted users, ask whether they accepted the chat or started a remote session, check endpoint logs for Quick Assist or unsanctioned remote tools after the chat and block the sender domain in Teams external access. Known false positives: real vendor help desks, managed service providers you chat with and partner display names ending in (Internal). Known limitation: the tenant list is a snapshot because the actors rotate tenants, so the display name match carries most of the weight over time. MessageEvents is populated by Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Hunting query, not an alert.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert
let Lookback = 7d;
let IocTenantDomains = dynamic(["supportedge33.onmicrosoft.com", "supportedge39.onmicrosoft.com", "helpdeskteam365.onmicrosoft.com", "itendpoint365.onmicrosoft.com", "itcoreportal.onmicrosoft.com", "networkadmin797.onmicrosoft.com", "networkadmin916.onmicrosoft.com", "itadmin922.onmicrosoft.com", "supportagentonline.onmicrosoft.com", "threatpro.onmicrosoft.com", "ithelpplus42.onmicrosoft.com", "corporateitservicellc.onmicrosoft.com", "techsupport2337.onmicrosoft.com"]);
MessageEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where IsExternalThread == true
| extend SenderDomain = tolower(tostring(split(SenderEmailAddress, "@")[1]))
| mv-expand Recipient = RecipientDetails
| extend RecipientAddress = tolower(tostring(Recipient.RecipientSmtpAddress))
| extend RecipientDomain = tostring(split(RecipientAddress, "@")[1])
| where isnotempty(SenderDomain) and SenderDomain != RecipientDomain
| extend LureName = SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help ?desk|\bit (service|support|tech|helpdesk)|service desk|supporte ti|it-representative|maintenance service|\(internal\))"
| extend IocTenant = SenderDomain in (IocTenantDomains)
| where LureName or IocTenant
| summarize Messages = dcount(TeamsMessageId), Recipients = dcount(RecipientAddress), Threads = dcount(ThreadId), DisplayNames = make_set(SenderDisplayName, 5), ThreatVerdicts = make_set(ThreatTypes, 5), IocTenantMessages = countif(IocTenant), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by SenderEmailAddress, SenderDomain
| extend KnownIndicatorTenant = IocTenantMessages > 0
| project Timestamp = LastSeen, FirstSeen, SenderEmailAddress, SenderDomain, DisplayNames, Messages, Recipients, Threads, KnownIndicatorTenant, ThreatVerdicts
| order by KnownIndicatorTenant desc, Recipients desc, Messages desc

name: M365 Token Replay Hunt: Campaign Addresses, Scripted Office Clients, Device Registration and Session Changes
desc: Hunts for the Microsoft 365 token replay campaign reported between July and September 2026, where tokens stolen through AiTM relays and device code phishing were replayed instead of guessing passwords. Three signals are combined. The first is a sign-in from the reported replay addresses, including the 193.26.115.0/24 range. The second is a scripted client (node or a bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent) using an Office client app ID, or any access to the Device Registration Service, from an IP the account has not used in the previous 14 days. The third is one session ID seen from more than one OS platform and more than one IP inside the lookback. Error codes 50133 and 53003 are included so that failed replays show up. MITRE ATT&CK: T1550.001 (Application Access Token), T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts), T1098.005 (Device Registration). SOC action: revoke sessions and reset the password, review registered devices and authentication methods because a reset alone leaves attacker devices and MFA methods in place, then check for new hidden inbox rules. Known false positives: users on VPN or roaming between networks and scripts that legitimately use Office clients. Known limitation: IOC addresses age quickly and the Office app IDs and the Device Registration Service ID are Microsoft first party IDs that normal traffic also uses, so treat hits as leads. Requires the EntraIdSignInEvents table in Defender advanced hunting, which needs a Microsoft Entra ID P2 license. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: SQL Server Spawned Shells and Post Exploitation Tooling Hunt
desc: Hunts for command execution launched from the SQL Server service process and for the follow on steps attackers commonly run after gaining a shell there. The first signal is sqlservr.exe starting a shell, scripting host, download tool or reconnaissance binary. The second is certutil decoding a payload. The third is a registry hive save of SAM, SYSTEM or SECURITY. The fourth is a local account or group being added. A device is returned when sqlservr.exe spawns any listed tool, or when at least two of the four stages appear on the same device on the same day. MITRE ATT&CK: T1505.001 (SQL Stored Procedures), T1059.003 (Windows Command Shell), T1140 (Deobfuscate/Decode Files), T1003.002 (Security Account Manager), T1136.001 (Local Account). SOC action: isolate the host, review who holds sysadmin on the instance, disable xp_cmdshell where it is not needed and rotate service account credentials. Known false positives: database maintenance jobs, backup agents that run scripts from SQL Agent or administrators who add local accounts. Known limitation: this is a behavioral pattern and no public report documents these exact process events, so treat it as a lead generator. Hunting query, not an alert.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert
let Lookback = 14d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sqlservr.exe"
    or (FileName in~ ("certutil.exe", "reg.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe")
        and (ProcessCommandLine contains "decode" or ProcessCommandLine contains "save" or ProcessCommandLine contains "/add"))
| extend IsSqlShell = InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sqlservr.exe"
    and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe", "regsvr32.exe", "wmic.exe", "certutil.exe", "whoami.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "reg.exe", "curl.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| extend IsDecode = FileName =~ "certutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s[-/]decode"
| extend IsHiveSave = FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bsave\b.*(hklm|hkey_local_machine)\\(sam|system|security)([^\\\w]|$)"
| extend IsAccountAdd = FileName in~ ("net.exe", "net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(user|localgroup)\b.*\s/add\b"
| where IsSqlShell or IsDecode or IsHiveSave or IsAccountAdd
| summarize SqlShell = countif(IsSqlShell), Decode = countif(IsDecode), HiveSave = countif(IsHiveSave), AccountAdd = countif(IsAccountAdd),
    FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 5), Samples = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 5)
    by DeviceName, Day = bin(Timestamp, 1d)
| extend Stages = iff(SqlShell > 0, 1, 0) + iff(Decode > 0, 1, 0) + iff(HiveSave > 0, 1, 0) + iff(AccountAdd > 0, 1, 0)
| where SqlShell > 0 or Stages >= 2
| sort by Stages desc, SqlShell desc, LastSeen desc

name: Citrix NetScaler Syslog Hunt: Command Strings After NSPPE in Log Entries
desc: Hunts NetScaler syslog for entries where shell syntax or common command line tools follow the NSPPE marker, which is the pattern seen when attacker supplied text is written into appliance logs. The query searches both Syslog and CommonSecurityLog, URL decodes the message, requires the strings pitboss and NSPPE. It then tests the trailing text for command separators, substitution syntax, redirection and tools such as curl, wget, bash and base64. MITRE ATT&CK: T1190 (Exploit Public Facing Application), T1059.004 (Unix Shell). SOC action: treat a hit as a possible compromise of the appliance, preserve a copy of the logs, patch to a fixed build, rotate credentials the appliance handles and review outbound connections from it. Known false positives: administrators pasting commands into support sessions that get logged. Known limitation: NetScaler syslog must already be forwarded to Sentinel. An empty result does not prove an appliance is clean because logging may be incomplete or rotated. Requires Syslog or CommonSecurityLog. Hunting query, not an alert.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert
// Needs NetScaler syslog in Sentinel. Empty results do not prove an appliance is clean.
let Lookback = 14d;
union isfuzzy=true Syslog, CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| extend Msg = url_decode(strcat(tostring(column_ifexists("SyslogMessage", "")), " ", tostring(column_ifexists("Message", ""))))
| where Msg contains "pitboss" and Msg contains "NSPPE"
| extend Trailing = extract(@"NSPPE;?(.*)$", 1, Msg)
| where Trailing matches regex @"(?i)(\$\{IFS\}|\$\(|`|&&|\||;|>|<|\b(curl|wget|whoami|perl|python|bash|nc|chmod|tar|cat|base64)\b)"
| project TimeGenerated, Type, Computer = tostring(column_ifexists("Computer", "")), SourceIP = tostring(column_ifexists("SourceIP", "")), Trailing, Msg
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

name: Node.js Runtime Spawning Shells on Hosts Flagged for the Brotli Vulnerability Hunt
desc: Hunts for the Node.js runtime starting a shell, download tool or scripting host. Each result is marked with whether Defender Vulnerability Management lists CVE-2026-111497 on that device. Package managers and CI runners are filtered out of the parent command line so the remaining rows are Node processes that run commands outside of normal build tooling. Results on flagged devices sort first. MITRE ATT&CK: T1190 (Exploit Public Facing Application), T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter). SOC action: patch the Node runtime on flagged devices, then review the parent application and the command line of each hit. Known false positives: applications that shell out on purpose, such as build scripts, deployment tools and desktop apps built on Node. Known limitation: no public source documents the exact process events produced by exploitation, so the process pattern is a heuristic and the vulnerability flag only tells you the runtime version is affected. Requires Defender Vulnerability Management data. Hunting query, not an alert.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert
let Lookback = 1d;
let VulnerableDevices = DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where CveId == "CVE-2026-111497"
    | summarize NodeVersions = make_set(SoftwareVersion, 5) by DeviceId;
let NodeRuntimes = dynamic(["node", "node.exe"]);
let ChildTools = dynamic(["sh", "bash", "dash", "zsh", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cscript.exe", "wscript.exe", "curl", "curl.exe", "wget", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "nc", "ncat"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (NodeRuntimes)
| where FileName in~ (ChildTools)
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\\/\s])(npm|npx|yarn|pnpm)(-cli)?([.]cmd|[.]c?js)?(\s|[""']|$)")
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)_work.?_actions")
| join kind=leftouter VulnerableDevices on DeviceId
| extend TvmFlaggedVulnerable = isnotempty(NodeVersions)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, TvmFlaggedVulnerable, NodeVersions = tostring(NodeVersions), AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by TvmFlaggedVulnerable desc, Timestamp desc

name: Authenticated SMTP Password Spray Hunt: Many Failures from Many IPs and Success After Failures
desc: Hunts for accounts that receive many failed Authenticated SMTP sign-ins from many different source addresses in a day, which is how a spray against a legacy mail protocol looks when it is spread across a botnet. Failures are error 50126 and 50053. An account is returned at 20 or more failures from 10 or more addresses. A flag shows whether any success occurred on the same account on the same day. MITRE ATT&CK: T1110.003 (Password Spraying), T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts). SOC action: for any account with a success, reset the password, revoke sessions and check mailbox rules and sent items, then block Authenticated SMTP for accounts that do not need it. Known false positives: a mail relay or scanner that retries with a stale password. Known limitation: thresholds are starting points and need tuning. The query only sees tenants where SMTP sign-ins are logged. Requires SigninLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: Phishing Email Followed by Sign In from a New IP Within 24 Hours Hunt
desc: Hunts for users who received a phishing email that was delivered or junked and then had a successful sign-in from an IP address they have not used in the previous 30 days, within 24 hours of the email. Interactive and non interactive sign-ins are both checked. Sign-ins from a country the user has not used before are counted separately. Users are ranked by new country sign-ins and then by the shortest time between the email and the sign-in. MITRE ATT&CK: T1566 (Phishing), T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts), T1539 (Steal Web Session Cookie). SOC action: confirm the sign-in with the user, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, reset the password and review registered authentication methods and inbox rules. Known false positives: travel, VPN changes and mobile networks on a user who also received an unrelated phishing email. Known limitation: users with no sign-in history in the baseline window are skipped. Run in the Defender portal with the Sentinel workspace connected, because the query joins Defender and Sentinel tables. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: Tensorlake Package Supply Chain Hunt: Token Monitor Persistence, Install Scripts and Campaign Domain
desc: Hunts for artifacts of the compromised Tensorlake package release across three tables. File events look for the reported SHA256 values and the gh-token-monitor service, script and launch agent names. Process events look for Node or Bun running the install script, any command line mentioning the token monitor or a scheduled task or PowerShell run of monitor.ps1. Network events look for connections to the reported campaign domain and for Node or Bun connecting to three public Ethereum RPC hosts. All signals are returned in one list with the signal type. MITRE ATT&CK: T1195.002 (Compromise Software Supply Chain), T1552.001 (Credentials In Files), T1053 (Scheduled Task/Job). SOC action: remove the package, rotate GitHub tokens and any secrets present on the host, delete the persistence files and review recent repository activity for the affected tokens. Known false positives: none expected for the hashes or the domain. The RPC hosts are harmless on their own and count only when Node or Bun makes the connection, so a legitimate Web3 application can match. The monitor name match can hit unrelated tooling that uses the same words. Known limitation: indicators are specific to one release and age quickly. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: LiteLLM Compromised Release Hunt: Install Command, Stealer Files and Attacker Hosts
desc: Hunts for installation and execution traces of the compromised LiteLLM release. Process events look for an install command that pins version 1.107.0. File events look for the cook.pth file in a site-packages folder, files with the .pc_once_ prefix, the remote_code_loader.lock file and the reported SHA256 values. Network events look for connections to the attacker host and the reported raw content path. Results are grouped by device and signal with sample details. MITRE ATT&CK: T1195.002 (Compromise Software Supply Chain), T1555 (Credentials from Password Stores), T1041 (Exfiltration Over C2 Channel). SOC action: remove the release, rebuild environments from a clean image, rotate every API key and cloud credential that was reachable from the host, then review outbound traffic from CI runners. Known false positives: low, since the file names and hashes are specific to this release. Known limitation: the install command signal only catches a pinned version typed on the command line, so a version resolved from a requirements file shows up only through the file and network signals. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: AhsayCBS Exploitation Hunt: Backup Service Child Processes and Cryptominer Staging
desc: Hunts for exploitation of the AhsayCBS backup server followed by cryptominer staging. Process events flag curl, certutil, powershell or cmd started by cbssvcX64.exe, plus command lines naming Taskgmr.ps1 or WinRing0x64.sys. File events look for the reported SHA256 values, the Taskgmr.ps1 script and the WinRing0x64.sys driver in a Temp folder. Network events look for the reported campaign addresses, the cloud storage host used for staging and the mining pool host. Results are grouped by device and signal. MITRE ATT&CK: T1190 (Exploit Public Facing Application), T1496 (Resource Hijacking), T1105 (Ingress Tool Transfer). SOC action: isolate the server, remove the miner and driver, patch AhsayCBS, rotate credentials stored on the backup server and review the integrity of the backup data. Known false positives: low for the hashes and hosts. Known limitation: the child process rule covers curl, certutil, powershell and cmd only, so other child processes need a separate review. Indicator addresses age quickly. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: Password Spray Hunt: Distributed Failures Across Many Accounts and Reported Spray Addresses
desc: Hunts for a source address that fails against many accounts inside a ten minute window, with the failure ratio, lockout count, scripted clients and any success from the same address. A source is returned when it fails against 10 or more accounts with at least 30 failures and a failure ratio of 0.5 or higher, or when it is one of four reported spray addresses and has any failure. A success after failures sorts first. Scripted clients are python-requests, python-urllib and curl user agents. MITRE ATT&CK: T1110.003 (Password Spraying), T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts). SOC action: for accounts with a success, reset the password, revoke sessions and confirm that multifactor authentication applied, then block the source in Conditional Access named locations. Known false positives: shared egress addresses such as corporate proxies and VPN gateways during a mass password expiry. Known limitation: the reported addresses age quickly. A slow spray that stays under the thresholds is not caught. Requires the EntraIdSignInEvents table in Defender advanced hunting, which needs a Microsoft Entra ID P2 license. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: Key Vault Secret Read Spike Hunt: Identity Reading Secrets from Many Vaults
desc: Hunts for an identity that reads secrets from three or more different Key Vaults with at least ten successful reads in a day, where that count exceeds the most vaults the same identity touched on any single day in the previous 14 days. Successful SecretGet and SecretList operations are counted. The result includes the account type, the application ID, the vaults touched, the source addresses and the user agents. MITRE ATT&CK: T1555 (Credentials from Password Stores), T1552.001 (Credentials In Files), T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts). SOC action: confirm with the owner of the identity, review the access policies or role assignments on each vault, rotate the secrets that were read and check the source addresses against the identity's usual locations. Known false positives: deployment pipelines and configuration services that legitimately read many vaults or new identities with no baseline. Known limitation: a slow read of one vault at a time stays under the vault count and is not caught. Requires the CloudKeyVaultEvents table in Defender advanced hunting. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: Linux Web Server Account Starting su, Root Shells or Namespace Tools Hunt
desc: Hunts for processes started by a web server account on Linux that point to a privilege escalation attempt. The accounts checked are www-data, apache, nginx, httpd, wwwrun, php-fpm and lsws. A row is returned when such an account starts su, when it starts a shell that runs as root, or when it starts unshare. Results are grouped by device and signal with the parent processes and sample command lines. MITRE ATT&CK: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation), T1059.004 (Unix Shell), T1505.003 (Web Shell). SOC action: isolate the host, look for a web shell in the web root, review the request logs around the first event and check for new root owned files or accounts. Known false positives: management panels and cron jobs that run helper scripts under a web account. Known limitation: no public source documents these exact process events, so the pattern is a heuristic. A kernel exploit that runs inside the original process produces no child process at all. Requires Defender for Endpoint on Linux. Hunting query, not an alert.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert
let WebAccounts = dynamic(["www-data", "apache", "nginx", "httpd", "wwwrun", "php-fpm", "lsws"]);
let ShellNames = dynamic(["sh", "bash", "dash", "zsh"]);
let Hunt = (T: (Timestamp: datetime, DeviceName: string, FolderPath: string, FileName: string, ProcessCommandLine: string, AccountName: string, InitiatingProcessAccountName: string, InitiatingProcessFileName: string)) {
    T
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FolderPath startswith "/"
    | where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ (WebAccounts)
    | extend Signal = case(
        FileName =~ "su", "su started by web account",
        FileName in~ (ShellNames) and AccountName =~ "root", "root shell under web account",
        FileName =~ "unshare", "namespace tool started by web account",
        "")
    | where isnotempty(Signal)
    | summarize
        Events = count(),
        FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
        LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
        Parents = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5),
        Commands = make_set(substring(ProcessCommandLine, 0, 200), 5)
        by DeviceName, Signal, WebAccount = InitiatingProcessAccountName
    | project Timestamp = LastSeen, DeviceName, Signal, WebAccount, Events, FirstSeen, Parents, Commands
    | order by Timestamp desc
};
Hunt(DeviceProcessEvents)

name: Qubole AWS Cross Account Access Hunt: Reported Account, Actor Principal, Session Names and Source Addresses
desc: Hunts CloudTrail for access linked to a reported compromise of the Qubole integration account. Rows match on a reported source address or the IPv6 prefix, the reported actor principal ID, a role session name starting with quiam-, an AssumeRole call from the reported account ID, or a GetCallerIdentity call with a TruffleHog user agent. A Matched column lists which signals fired. MITRE ATT&CK: T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts), T1550 (Use Alternate Authentication Material), T1552 (Unsecured Credentials). SOC action: review the trust policy of every role that allows the reported account, rotate any external IDs, limit roles to least privilege and review what the sessions did after the AssumeRole. Known false positives: the same AssumeRole pattern appears in legitimate integration traffic, so review the source address and the session name before escalating. Known limitation: the account ID and addresses are indicators from one report. Requires the AWSCloudTrail table from the AWS connector. Hunting query, not an alert.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert
// AssumeRole from the Qubole account also appears in legitimate integration traffic. Review the source address and session name.
let QuboleAccount = "805246085872";
let ActorPrincipal = "AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS";
let QuboleIPs = dynamic(["57.129.54.120", "2001:41d0:70d:7800::", "45.83.220.211", "185.209.199.73", "89.37.63.175"]);
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
| where SourceIpAddress in (QuboleIPs)
    or SourceIpAddress startswith "2001:41d0:70d:7800:"
    or UserIdentityPrincipalid == ActorPrincipal
    or UserIdentityArn contains "/quiam-"
    or UserAgent has "TruffleHog"
    or (EventName == "AssumeRole" and (UserIdentityAccountId == QuboleAccount or RequestParameters contains "quiam-"))
| extend Matched = trim_end(";", strcat(
    iff(SourceIpAddress in (QuboleIPs) or SourceIpAddress startswith "2001:41d0:70d:7800:", "IOCSourceIP;", ""),
    iff(UserIdentityPrincipalid == ActorPrincipal, "ActorPrincipal;", ""),
    iff(UserIdentityArn contains "/quiam-" or (EventName == "AssumeRole" and RequestParameters matches regex @'"roleSessionName"\s*:\s*"quiam-'), "SessionName;", ""),
    iff(EventName == "AssumeRole" and UserIdentityAccountId == QuboleAccount, "QuboleAccountAssumeRole;", ""),
    iff(EventName == "GetCallerIdentity" and UserAgent has "TruffleHog", "TruffleHogValidation;", "")))
| extend SessionName = coalesce(
    extract(@'"roleSessionName"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"', 1, RequestParameters),
    extract(@'/(quiam-[^/]+)$', 1, UserIdentityArn))
| where isnotempty(Matched)
| project TimeGenerated, Matched, EventName, SourceIpAddress, UserIdentityAccountId, UserIdentityPrincipalid, UserIdentityArn, SessionName, RecipientAccountId, AWSRegion, UserAgent, ErrorCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

name: ESXi Implant Hunt on Firewall Logs: Reported Addresses and Port Bursts
desc: Hunts perimeter or upstream firewall logs for the GhostFrame ESXi implant, which disables the host firewall and so leaves no trace in host logs. A one minute window is returned when a source or destination matches a reported address, when one pair of hosts touches five or more of six ports the implant uses (53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443, 9443), or both. A Matched column shows which rule applied. MITRE ATT&CK: T1562.004 (Disable or Modify System Firewall), T1021 (Remote Services), T1571 (Non Standard Port). SOC action: isolate the ESXi host from the network, collect the host for forensics, rotate root and vCenter credentials and review guest machines on the host. Known false positives: port scanners, vulnerability scans and monitoring that probes several of these ports. Known limitation: the port burst rule is a heuristic and the addresses age quickly. Requires CommonSecurityLog from a firewall connector. Hunting query, not an alert.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert
// Run on perimeter or upstream firewall logs. The implant disables the ESXi host firewall.
let GhostFramePorts = dynamic([53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443, 9443]);
let GhostFrameIPs = dynamic(["193.5.65.114", "45.158.196.81", "45.158.196.141"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationPort in (GhostFramePorts) or SourceIP in (GhostFrameIPs) or DestinationIP in (GhostFrameIPs)
| summarize
    PortCount = dcountif(DestinationPort, DestinationPort in (GhostFramePorts)),
    Ports = make_set_if(DestinationPort, DestinationPort in (GhostFramePorts)),
    IOCEvents = countif(SourceIP in (GhostFrameIPs) or DestinationIP in (GhostFrameIPs)),
    Connections = count(),
    Actions = make_set(DeviceAction, 5),
    Vendors = make_set(DeviceVendor, 3),
    Products = make_set(DeviceProduct, 3)
    by SourceIP, DestinationIP, Window = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| extend Ports = array_sort_asc(Ports)
| extend Matched = case(
    IOCEvents > 0 and PortCount >= 5, "IOCAddressAndPortBurst",
    IOCEvents > 0, "IOCAddress",
    PortCount >= 5, "PortBurst",
    "")
| where isnotempty(Matched)
| project Window, Matched, SourceIP, DestinationIP, PortCount, Ports, Connections, Actions, Vendors, Products
| order by Window desc

name: ARTEX Agentic Framework Artifacts Hunt: webhook.site Traffic, Probe Account Name and Known Web Shell Names
desc: Hunts for artifacts left by the ARTEX agentic attack framework in the last 30 days. Network events look for connections to webhook.site. Process events look for curl, PowerShell, cmd or wget command lines that mention webhook.site, and for the ArtexProbe account name anywhere in a command line. File events look for files starting with artex-probe- and for the web shell names cl1217.jsp, f1219a.jsp and z1219.jsp. Results are grouped by device and signal with sample details. MITRE ATT&CK: T1190 (Exploit Public Facing Application), T1505.003 (Web Shell), T1567 (Exfiltration Over Web Service). SOC action: isolate the host, remove the files, check the web application that served them for the entry point, review accounts named like the probe account and block webhook.site where there is no business use. Known false positives: developers and testers who use webhook.site on purpose. Known limitation: the file and account names are specific to the reported activity and are easy for an operator to change. Hunting query, not an alert.

name: GSocket Activity and Web Server Script Download on Linux Hunt
desc: Hunts Linux devices for GSocket tooling and for the behavior that usually surrounds a web server compromise. Process events look for gs-netcat and gsocket names, the systemd-remount-d masquerade, the reported SHA256 values and command lines naming the GSocket hosts. They also flag a web server or PHP runtime piping a download into a shell, execution from hidden folders under /dev/shm and exec -a names that imitate kernel threads. File events look for the GSocket artifact names and hashes, hidden staging under /dev/shm and a web server process writing to cron, systemd or shell profile paths. Network events look for the reported GSocket hosts. Each row carries an Evidence label. MITRE ATT&CK: T1190 (Exploit Public Facing Application), T1059.004 (Unix Shell), T1036.004 (Masquerade Task or Service), T1053.003 (Cron). SOC action: isolate the host, review the web application for the entry point, remove the persistence entries and rotate credentials stored on the server. Known false positives: installer scripts that a web server runs on purpose and browsers that create hidden folders under /dev/shm. Known limitation: hashes and hosts age quickly and the behavioral labels are heuristics. Requires Defender for Endpoint on Linux. Hunting query, not an alert.
kql:
// Hunting query, not an alert
let GSocketHashes = dynamic([
    "d94f75a70b5cabaf786ac57177ed841732e62bdcc9a29e06e5b41d9be567bcfa",
    "f95c4d029e6784e3849b4d1e2e2ae1a661187236ef7c5d487c71158a290a03b5",
    "55d141bb2f62c527c3fea3413b8429fed7d52633d0b123b5e611bfa42165229f",
    "12450bafc7a4398040e1ad3a16dbf4dbc79b6a8f83ef306c4f0f73f59886f06c"]);
let GSocketHosts = dynamic(["gsocket.io", "gsgg.b-cdn.net"]);
let WebRuntime = dynamic(["apache2", "httpd", "nginx", "php", "php-fpm", "php-cgi", "lsphp", "java", "node", "tomcat", "gunicorn", "uwsgi", "caddy"]);
let IsWeb = (name:string) { name in~ (WebRuntime) or name startswith "php" or name startswith "lsphp" };
union
(
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d) and FolderPath startswith "/"
    | extend Evidence = case(
        FileName contains "gs-netcat" or FileName contains "gsocket" or FileName =~ "systemd-remount-d" or SHA256 in~ (GSocketHashes)
            or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gs-netcat", "gsnetcat", "gsocket.io", "gsgg.b-cdn.net"), "GSocketTooling",
        (IsWeb(InitiatingProcessFileName) or IsWeb(InitiatingProcessParentFileName))
            and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @'(curl|wget)\b[^|]*\|\s*(ba|da|z)?sh\b|\b((ba|da|z)?sh|eval|source)\s+(-c\s+)?[\x22\x27]?(<\(|\$\()\s*(curl|wget)\b', "WebServerDownloadExecute",
        FolderPath startswith "/dev/shm/" and FolderPath contains "/.", "HiddenShmExecution",
        ProcessCommandLine matches regex @'(?i)exec\s+-a\s+\S*\[[a-z0-9/:_-]+\]', "KernelThreadNameMasquerade",
        "")
    | where isnotempty(Evidence)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Evidence, Indicator = FolderPath, Detail = ProcessCommandLine, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
),
(
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d) and FolderPath startswith "/"
    | extend Evidence = case(
        FolderPath startswith "/dev/shm/.gs-" or FileName in~ ("systemd-remount-d", ".gsn_ora", "defunct", "defunct.service") or SHA256 in~ (GSocketHashes), "GSocketArtifact",
        ActionType == "FileCreated" and FolderPath startswith "/dev/shm/" and FolderPath contains "/."
                and not(FolderPath startswith_cs "/dev/shm/.org.chromium." or FolderPath startswith_cs "/dev/shm/.com.google."), "HiddenShmStaging",
        ActionType == "FileCreated" and (IsWeb(InitiatingProcessFileName) or IsWeb(InitiatingProcessParentFileName))
            and (FolderPath matches regex @"^/(etc/cron|etc/systemd/system|usr/lib/systemd/system|var/spool/cron)" or FileName in~ (".bashrc", ".profile", ".bash_profile", ".zshrc")), "WebServerPersistence",
        "")
    | where isnotempty(Evidence)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Evidence, Indicator = FolderPath, Detail = ActionType, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
),
(
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | extend Evidence = case(RemoteUrl has_any (GSocketHosts), "GSocketHost", "")
    | where isnotempty(Evidence)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Evidence, Indicator = RemoteUrl, Detail = strcat(RemoteIP, ":", tostring(RemotePort)), AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by Timestamp desc
